name: Safety Switch String — Finding the Open Switch
summary: Isolate which switch in a series safety chain is open, one switch at a time, without chasing the whole string with a voltmeter.

requires: The equipment's wiring diagram, usually inside the blower door
A voltage tester rated for line voltage — NOT this instrument

safety: Kill power at the disconnect and at the breaker, lock out and tag out. Verify absence of line voltage with a properly rated tester. This device is NOT a CAT-rated mains meter.
Never ohm a live circuit. If the string is energised your readings are wrong and you can damage the control board.
A rollout switch that has tripped is telling you flame has escaped the heat exchanger. Do NOT simply reset it and leave. Find and fix the cause — this is a carbon monoxide hazard.
A cracked heat exchanger, blocked flue or failed inducer are life-safety faults. If you are not qualified to condemn or repair combustion equipment, stop and call someone who is.
Do not jumper out a safety switch to make the equipment run, even briefly for testing. Every one of these switches exists because somebody was hurt.

notes: Continuity and resistance are trustworthy on this firmware. A closed switch reads near zero, an open switch reads OL, and both results are dependable.
Zero the leads with REL (AUTO button) before measuring closed switches — you want to distinguish a genuinely low-resistance contact from a pitted one.
Use the Chart layout (OK cycles Full > Chart > Stats) when checking a switch that is suspected of being intermittent, so a momentary open is visible after the fact.
The continuity beeper gives you a hands-free result while you are working inside a cabinet.

instructions.text: Find the safety string on the wiring diagram and list every switch in it, in order. Typically: door interlock, high limit, rollout switch or switches, blocked-vent (spill) switch, pressure switch, and on cooling equipment the condensate float switch.
instructions.expect: A written list. You are going to check each one individually.

instructions.text: Kill power, lock out, and verify absence of line voltage in the cabinet with a rated tester.
Select Continuity with LEFT/RIGHT. Touch the probes together and press AUTO to zero the leads.
Disconnect ONE lead from the first switch in the list, so you are measuring that switch alone and not the rest of the string.
Measure across the switch terminals. Record closed (near zero, beeper sounds) or open (OL).
instructions.expect: A definite result, not a marginal one.

instructions.text: Reconnect and move to the next switch. Work through the whole list before drawing a conclusion — more than one switch can be open.
instructions.expect: Every switch in the string characterised.

instructions.text: Interpret against what each switch is SUPPOSED to do at rest. This is where most people go wrong: some of these switches are normally open when the equipment is off, and finding them open is not a fault. See the knowledge base.
instructions.expect: You know which open readings are normal and which are not.

instructions.text: For any switch that is genuinely open when it should be closed, find the cause before resetting or replacing anything.
instructions.expect: A physical explanation: a blocked drain, a dirty filter, a failed inducer, a plugged flue, a heat exchanger problem.

instructions.text: For a switch that reads closed but with noticeable resistance, look at the contacts and the terminals. A limit switch that reads a couple of ohms is on its way out.

measurements.label: A switch that should be closed
measurements.fail: OL means that switch is open — it is either tripped or failed. Above about 1 ohm means pitted contacts or a corroded terminal; it may still pass current now and fail under load later.

measurements.label: A switch that is normally open at rest
measurements.expect: OL, and that is CORRECT. The pressure switch and any similar draft-proving switch is open until the inducer creates draft.
measurements.fail: A normally-open switch reading closed at rest is stuck closed — a serious fault, because the control is being told there is draft when there is none.

measurements.label: Condensate float switch
measurements.expect: Closed (continuity) when the pan is empty and the float is down.
measurements.fail: Open with a dry pan means a failed switch or a stuck float. Open with a wet pan means the drain is blocked — clear the drain, do not blame the switch.

measurements.label: Rollout switch
measurements.fail: Open means flame rolled out of the burner compartment. This is a combustion fault and a carbon monoxide hazard. Most rollout switches are manual reset specifically so that a technician has to look at the equipment before it runs again. Find the cause.

measurements.label: High limit switch
measurements.fail: Open on a cold furnace means the switch has failed. Repeatedly tripping when hot means restricted airflow — dirty filter, closed registers, undersized return, or a failing blower. Replacing the limit without fixing airflow just moves the failure.

measurements.label: Blower door interlock
measurements.expect: Closed when the plunger is depressed.
measurements.fail: An intermittent door switch produces a furnace that works while you are standing there with the door off and dies when you put it back on. It is a genuinely common and genuinely annoying fault.

knowledge_base.why_one_switch_at_a_time: A series safety string with one open switch reads open end to end, and every switch downstream of the open one has no voltage across it. Chasing that with a voltmeter means walking the string looking for where the voltage disappears, on a live circuit, inside a cabinet with line voltage in it. Ohming each switch individually, dead, is faster, safer and unambiguous.
knowledge_base.the_pressure_switch_trap: The single most common misdiagnosis in this whole procedure is condemning a pressure switch because it reads open with the equipment off. It is SUPPOSED to be open. It is a normally-open switch that closes only when the inducer motor pulls enough negative pressure. If the equipment fails on pressure switch, the fault is far more often the inducer, a blocked flue or intake, a cracked or disconnected hose, a plugged pressure port, or water in the condensate trap of a high-efficiency unit. Check those before you order a switch.
knowledge_base.why_a_switch_opened: These switches are sensors, not consumables. A tripped limit means the furnace got too hot, which almost always means airflow. A tripped rollout means combustion products came out of the burner box, which means a blockage, a cracked heat exchanger, or a venting problem. A tripped float means water backed up. Replacing a tripped safety without finding the cause is how equipment ends up hurting somebody.
knowledge_base.manual_vs_auto_reset: Auto-reset switches close again when they cool, so a furnace with an airflow problem short-cycles. Manual-reset switches — most rollouts, some limits — stay open deliberately. If you find a manual-reset switch tripped, someone has to press it, and that someone should have already found out why.
knowledge_base.marginal_contacts: A switch reading a couple of ohms instead of near zero is carrying current through a small, pitted contact area. Under load it heats, its resistance rises further, and eventually it drops out — usually on the coldest night of the year. Zeroing your leads first is what lets you see the difference between 0.1 ohm and 2 ohms.
knowledge_base.related_modules: If the safety string is intact and the equipment still will not run, check the thermostat cable next — see hvac/thermostat_wiring_check.
